subject: body
title: Brain and Nerves
about: The brain as the boss of thinking, feeling, remembering and moving, nerves that carry messages like tiny wires, the spinal cord inside the backbone, the super-fast reflex, how practice builds new brain connections, a brain that keeps working through sleep and dreams, why it is wrinkly, and what protects it: a cushion of liquid inside the skull and a helmet on wheels. Inside-the-body anatomy is a bridge topic beyond NC Grade 1; the nearest codes are 1.PCH.2.1 (avoiding injury, the helmet), 1.MEH.1.2 (feelings start in the brain) and 1.MEH.2.1 (trying again when something is hard: the practice and try-again cards). Read it together: the tablet reads every card aloud while he tries the hot-pan reflex story and the left-brain, right-hand trick.
tip: Ask him to wiggle one toe and talk through the trip: brain, down the backbone, along a nerve, to the toe muscle.

cards.q: Which part of your body is the boss that tells all the other parts what to do?
cards.note: The brain runs thinking, feeling, remembering and moving. It even keeps you breathing.

cards.q: Messages race between your brain and the rest of you along tiny wires. What are they called?
cards.note: Nerves reach every part of you, from your scalp to your toes.

cards.q: A thick bundle of nerves runs down inside your backbone. What is it called?
cards.note: The backbone protects the spinal cord the way the skull protects the brain. Messages run up and down it.

cards.q: Something soft and fluffy brushes your hand. Where does that touch message travel to?
cards.note: Skin nerves send the message up the spinal cord, and the brain decides: soft! Then it may tell your hand to pet it again.

cards.q: You touch a hot pan and your hand jerks away before you even think. What is that called?
cards.note: A reflex is a super-fast shortcut. The spinal cord answers before the brain even hears about it.

cards.q: How fast do nerves carry their messages?
cards.note: Some nerve messages travel more than 200 miles an hour, faster than a race car.

cards.q: A balloon pops and you jump. What does your brain tell your heart to do?
cards.note: Feelings start in the brain, and a quick heartbeat gets you ready to move. Slow breaths tell the brain all is well.

cards.q: You practice tying your shoes. What is your brain building each time?
cards.note: Practice makes brain paths stronger, like a trail you walk every day. Mistakes help build them too.

cards.q: You get a puzzle wrong, then try again. What is your brain doing?
cards.note: Trying again is how the brain learns. Every try makes the path a little clearer.

cards.q: Late at night you are fast asleep. What is your brain doing?
cards.note: At night the brain sorts the day, keeps you breathing and makes dreams.

cards.q: The pictures and stories you see while you sleep are called...?
cards.note: Dreams are your brain playing while you rest. You dream most in the hours near morning.

cards.q: You tumble off your bike and your helmet bumps the ground. What did the helmet do for your brain?
cards.note: The skull is hard, but a hard fall can still shake the brain, so the helmet squashes a little and takes the bump instead. After a big bump a grown-up should check the helmet.

cards.q: The outside of your brain is wrinkly, with lots of folds. Why?
cards.note: The folds pack a big thinking surface into a small skull, like crumpling a big sheet of paper into a ball.

cards.q: Your brain is made of billions of tiny...?
cards.note: They are called neurons, and each one can talk to thousands of others. That is how you think.

cards.q: Your brain has a left half and a right half. The left half controls which hand?
cards.note: The wires cross over. The left half of your brain runs the right side of your body, and the right half runs the left.

cards.q: Inside your skull, your brain floats in a little clear liquid. What is the liquid for?
cards.note: The liquid works like a cushion, so a bump on the head does not shake the brain hard. A helmet adds even more cushion.
